newsitem.title: USA: Eight percent mortgage is back after six months.
newsitem.headline: Eight percent mortgage is back after six months.

text.p: The 8 percent home mortgage is back this week for the first time in six months, as overall interest rates shot up after the Federal Reserve tightened credit, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 8.18 percent in the week ending April 4, the highest since 8.28 percent in the Sept. 13, 1996.
The 8 percent mortgage was last seen during the week ended Oct. 4 when the 30-year loan averaged 8.06 percent. Last week's 30-year rate was 7.97 percent.
Fifteen-year fixed-rate mortgages climbed to an average 7.70 percent, the highest since 7.81 percent in the Sept. 13, 1996 week. Last week's 15-year rate averaged 7.48 percent, Freddie Mac said.
One-year adjustable mortgage rates inched upward to 5.80 percent, the highest since 5.82 percent in the week ended Sept. 27, 1996. This compares with 5.71 percent last week.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.78 percent, the 15-year 7.29 percent and the adjustable loan 5.62 percent.

"This week's interest rates further reflect the rate hike by the Fed, but the survey also incorporates the reaction to the strong home sales figures," Robert Van Order, Freddie Mac chief economist, said.
"The employment figures will be released tomorrow and that will certainly influence next week's survey results."
Last month, the Fed increased the federal funds rate by a quarter-percentage point, causing a rippling increase in interest rates.
The National Association of Realtors last week said U.S. February sales of existing homes rose 9 percent to an annualized rate of 4.26 million units.
On Friday, the Labour Department will issue U.S. employment data for March.
Lenders charged an average of 1.7 percent in fees and points on both 30- and 15-year loans, down from 1.8 percent last week. They charged 1.4 percent on adjustable loans, unchanged from last week.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
